chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Nadr from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) would make easy for the muqatib (slave seeking manumission by installment), for they did not stipulate that if he became unable [to pay], he would remain a slave. And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Their stipulation holds.' And he said: 'The muqatib is waited for for three periods (of payment). If he becomes unable, he is returned to slavery.'

The solution in these narrations is one of two things: one is that they came in agreement with the general public (Ahl al-Sunnah) and according to what they narrate from Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him), for they narrate from him that he said: 'When the muqatib pays something, he is freed from it in proportion to what he paid,' and they do not distinguish between whether the condition is fulfilled or not. And his son (peace be upon him) clarified this in the narration of Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, which we presented at the beginning of the chapter.

The other solution is that it is to be understood as recommended (istihbab), for whoever waits for the muqatib for a year, or two years, or three years, or delays a period to another period, has much merit and abundant reward in that, even if it is not obligatory upon him.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.عَجَز: To become unable or insolvent (regarding payment)
key_terms.مُكَاتَب: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a certain sum for his freedom in installments

ai.seo_question: What are the jurisprudential rules for a slave buying their freedom in installments (mukataba) if they fail to pay?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent discrepancy between the strict legal ruling (that failure to pay results in re-enslavement) and the practice of Imam al-Sadiq by distinguishing between obligatory strictness and recommended leniency. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of *istihsan* (juristic preference), where masters are encouraged to grant extended time (*takhir*) to slaves, viewing such patience as a source of abundant spiritual reward rather than a binding legal requirement.
